insights:
The most glaring problem with this algorithm is its extreme passivity: 124 out of 150 trials (82.7%) produced NO trades. In the last 10 trials, 9 out of 10 were no-trade days, and the single trade taken (MRVL long in Trial 142) was actually a winner at +1.9%. This means the algorithm is leaving massive amounts of alpha on the table. The threshold and/or conviction scoring pipeline is so restrictive that it refuses to act even in clearly directional regimes — Trial 146 had a 73% confidence risk-on regime with SPX +1.97% and Nasdaq +2.18%, and Trial 148 had a 90% confidence crisis regime, yet ZERO trades were generated in either. These are exactly the high-conviction environments where the algorithm should be deploying capital aggressively. The algorithm appears to be optimizing for avoiding losses rather than capturing gains, which is a fundamental design flaw for a day trading system.

The dimension predictive power data reveals a troublingly narrow spread: all dimensions cluster between 69.1 and 72.5 out of 100. This near-uniform predictive power suggests the scoring system lacks discriminatory power — no single dimension is clearly separating winners from losers. Yet the weights have drifted dramatically, with catalystClarity at 21.3% and volumeLiquidity at only 10.2%, despite their predictive power being only ~3 points apart. The weight evolution shows catalystClarity has been monotonically increasing from 18% to 21.3% without strong empirical justification given the flat predictive power landscape. Meanwhile, timingUrgency (72.5 — the highest predictive dimension) has been bouncing between 8.3% and 18.6% and currently sits at only 11.5%. The weights are not tracking predictive power.

Looking at the best trials, every single one was a single-trade day with 100% win rate. This confirms the algorithm CAN pick winners when it acts — the issue is it almost never acts. The worst trials show a pattern: multi-trade days (Trial 75 with 3 trades, Trial 138 with 2) tend to perform poorly, suggesting the algorithm dilutes conviction when it takes multiple positions. Trial 30 (BRK.B short, score=0) and Trial 55 (SNOW long, score=15) suggest the algorithm occasionally takes contrarian positions that fail badly — shorting a defensive name or going long a high-beta growth stock without sufficient catalyst support.

The regime classification pipeline has a critical issue: it frequently classifies regimes with very low confidence (38-48%) and defaults to 'rotation' or 'range-bound', which then suppresses trade generation. In 7 of the last 10 trials, regime confidence was below 50%. The algorithm treats low-confidence regime classification as a reason not to trade, when it should instead be using regime uncertainty as a signal to reduce position size while still trading directional setups within the regime's dominant characteristic. Trial 145 (risk-off, 67% confidence) and Trial 148 (crisis, 90% confidence) were high-confidence regimes that should have generated short/defensive trades but produced nothing.

The profit factor of 21.71 on winning trades is extraordinarily high, which means when the algorithm does trade, it's highly selective and usually right. But a 30.8% win rate combined with only 26 trades in 150 trials means the system is generating maybe 5-8 actual gains over the entire period. The algorithm needs to trade 3-4x more frequently while maintaining selectivity. The path to improvement is NOT tightening filters further — it's loosening the composite threshold while adding regime-specific trade templates that automatically generate candidates in high-confidence directional regimes.
strategyChanges: CRITICAL: Implement regime-specific trade generation templates. When crisis regime confidence >75%, automatically generate short candidates in high-beta sectors (tech, discretionary, small-cap ETFs). When risk-on confidence >65%, automatically generate long candidates in momentum leaders. The current pipeline waits passively for candidates to exceed the threshold — it should actively seek regime-aligned trades.

REDUCE composite threshold from current effective level (~70-75 implied) to 58. The algorithm's 82.7% no-trade rate with 21.71 profit factor proves it is drastically over-filtering. At 58, expect trade frequency to increase to ~40-45% of days while maintaining edge.

ELIMINATE multi-trade days unless all trades are directionally aligned with the regime. Trial 75 (3 longs in a session that scored 5/100) and Trial 138 (2 shorts that both lost) show that multi-position days destroy capital. Cap at 2 trades max, same direction only, and require the second trade to exceed a higher threshold (composite + 5 points).

ADD a regime-confidence multiplier to marketAlignment. Currently marketAlignment is weighted at 18% but regime confidence is often below 50%, meaning the algorithm is uncertain about the environment. When regime confidence exceeds 70%, boost marketAlignment contribution by 1.3x. When below 40%, reduce it by 0.7x. This creates a dynamic weighting that responds to conviction about the macro environment.

IMPLEMENT forced-trade logic for extreme regimes: if crisis confidence >85% or risk-on confidence >75%, the system MUST generate at least one trade recommendation using regime-aligned ETFs (SPY/QQQ short for crisis, IWM/QQQ long for risk-on) as a fallback. The current system leaving 90% confidence crisis days with zero trades is inexcusable.
blindSpots: ETF/Index-level trades in directional regimes: The best trade in the dataset was IWM long in risk-on (Trial 1, score=100). The algorithm rarely recommends broad index trades despite them being the highest-conviction plays in directional regimes. It over-focuses on single-stock catalysts and misses the forest for the trees.

Short-side opportunities in high-stress environments: Trial 148 had stress=48 (highest in last 10) with 90% crisis confidence, yet no short trades were generated. The algorithm appears to have a long bias or insufficient short-candidate generation in risk-off/crisis regimes.

Earnings momentum plays: Several best trades (PLTR short, TGT short, UBER long, PNC long) appear to be earnings-related. The algorithm doesn't seem to have a systematic earnings catalyst detector that upgrades conviction on the day after significant earnings surprises.

Sector rotation trades: 5 of 10 recent trials classified as 'rotation' regime, but zero rotation-specific pair trades were generated. The algorithm identifies rotation but doesn't act on it — it should be generating long-sector-leader/short-sector-laggard pairs.

Volatility regime transitions: The algorithm misses the transition from range-bound/rotation into directional regimes. Trial 143 (risk-on 60%) followed by later rotation trials suggests the algorithm doesn't detect when rotation is resolving into a directional move.
pipelineIssues: SIGNAL GATHERING: The pipeline appears to generate insufficient trade candidates. In 82.7% of trials, either no candidates are generated or all candidates score below threshold. The candidate generation step needs to be decoupled from the scoring step — generate MORE candidates (10-15 per day minimum), then score and filter aggressively.

REGIME CLASSIFICATION: Rotation is used as a catch-all for ambiguous environments (5 of last 10 trials). The 'rotation' regime needs sub-classification: sector-rotation-bullish (cyclicals leading), sector-rotation-bearish (defensives leading), and true factor-rotation. Each sub-type should have different trade templates.

DAILY BRIEFING: The briefing narratives are reasonable but don't translate into actionable trade ideas. Trial 146's briefing correctly identified a 'powerful broad-based rally' but generated no trades. The briefing-to-recommendation handoff is broken — the briefing concludes with a narrative assessment but doesn't generate specific ticker-level hypotheses that feed into scoring.

TRADE RECOMMENDATION: The recommendation engine has an implicit veto that kills too many trades. Given the 21.71 profit factor on executed trades, the engine's selection ability is excellent — but its pass rate is catastrophically low. The veto logic needs to be relaxed, especially in high-confidence regimes.

OUTCOME SCORING: The scoring system awards 50 for no-trade days, which makes the median score 50 regardless of missed opportunities. This creates no penalty for inaction. Implement an 'opportunity cost' penalty: if the regime was high-confidence and the best regime-aligned ETF moved >1% in the predicted direction, deduct 10-15 points from the no-trade score. This will train the system to recognize that not trading in obvious environments is a failure.
